title: Rice Bug (Atangya): Damage, Thresholds and Control
metaTitle: Rice Bug: How to Spot and Control Atangya in Palay
metaDescription: The rice bug sucks milky grains and leaves palay empty and spotted. Learn its local names, when to count it, and when a spray is really worth it.
excerpt: The rice bug, Leptocorisa oratorius, is the slender, foul smelling insect that Tagalog farmers call atangya. It sucks the grains of palay (rice still in the husk) while they are still milky, and a heavy attack leaves panicles full of empty, spotted grains. This guide shows how to tell it from the black bug, when to count it, and when a spray really pays.

blocks.text: What the rice bug looks like

Most [rice insects](/problems/rice-insects) attack the leaves, the stems or the roots. This one waits for the grain. Adults are long and thin, with long legs and long antennae, and their color is greenish brown. The nymphs, or young bugs, have green bodies that blend with the leaves, so many farmers miss them.

Eggs sit in small batches along the midrib of the leaf. They are oval, shiny and reddish brown. Pick up an adult and you will know it at once, because it gives off a strong, bad smell. Adults feed in the early morning and late afternoon. Under bright sun they hide in grassy areas. When you disturb a hill, the nymphs drop to the lower part of the plant while the adults fly a short distance away.
Rice ear bug, atangya, tayangaw and alitangya

In English you will read about the rice bug, the rice ear bug or the rice earhead bug. PhilRice lists atangya as its Tagalog name and dangaw as its Ilocano name. One source from Camarines Sur gives tayangaw. We found no second source for it, so treat it as a local word. The general words for insects and bugs in Tagalog are kulisap and insekto, and our list of [farm words in Tagalog](/blog/farm-words-in-tagalog) has more.

Be careful with alitangya. Tagalog dictionaries, Wiktionary among them, give alitangya as the name of the rice black bug, the round, dark stink bug that PhilRice calls itim na atangya. PhilRice keeps plain atangya for the rice bug. Because the names overlap, trust the shape of the insect more than the name. A slender, long legged bug on the panicle is the rice bug. A broad, oval black bug at the base of the hill is the [rice black bug](/problems/rice-black-bug).

Both nymphs and adults push their mouthparts into the developing grain and suck out its contents. They feed from just before flowering up to the soft dough stage, and every soft, milky grain is at risk. PhilRice notes that the nymphs do more damage than the adults. Before the grains form, the bugs feed on young shoots and leaves, but the serious damage comes at the milky stage. IRRI says rice bugs can sometimes cut yield by as much as 30 percent.

items: Empty or unfilled grains, and small or shriveled ones
Deformed grains with brown or dark spots where the bugs fed
Panicles that stay erect in heavily infested fields, since light grains do not bend them
A bad smell in the raw and cooked rice, and straw that cattle refuse to eat

blocks.text: Nutrient deficiency and flower [thrips](/problems/thrips) can leave similar grains. So before you act, confirm the cause by finding the bugs, their eggs or their smell.

The bug lives in every rice environment, but it is more common in rainfed and upland rice. Between crops it lives on wild grasses, then it moves into rice fields when the crop flowers. It is less active during the dry season. Watch your field closely when:

items: Woodlands, weedy areas or wild grasses along canals sit next to your field
Farms around you plant at different times, so flowering fields follow one another for weeks
The monsoon rains begin, or the weather stays warm with overcast skies and frequent drizzles
The rainy season is ending, since IRRI says numbers rise at that time

blocks.text: How to count rice bugs and when to act

items.title: Start before flowering
items.text: Begin scouting just before the panicles come out and keep going every day until the hard dough stage. PhilRice puts the risky window at about 30 days, from flowering to soft dough.

items.title: Walk the field early or late
items.text: Go out in the early morning or late afternoon, when the bugs sit on the panicles. Walk diagonally across the field and check 20 hills.

items.title: Count every nymph and adult
items.text: Adults often fly off before you reach the hill, so your count may show mostly nymphs. Write the number down with the date and the lot.

items.title: Compare with the threshold
items.text: Consider a spray only when the count passes a threshold in the table below. The two sources count differently, since IRRI uses 20 hills and PhilRice uses a square meter. If your count stays under, keep counting instead of spraying.

blocks.caption: Action thresholds for atangya, as IRRI and PhilRice state them
rows: More than 5 nymphs and adults per square meter
More than 10 nymphs and adults per square meter

Cultural and natural control of atangya

items: **Clean the surroundings.** Cut grassy weeds in the field, on the pilapil (levees) and along canals, so the bugs have fewer places to breed between crops.
**Plant together.** PhilRice advises planting at the same time across the community after at least a month of fallow, so bugs cannot move from early fields to late ones.
**Keep the crop even.** A level field with even fertilizer and water grows at one pace, so the whole lot passes the milky stage together.
**Net them.** Sweeping with a net in the early morning or late afternoon works when numbers are low, though it takes labor.
**Bait them.** PhilRice lists rotting meat, fish or snails as baits that draw the bugs to one spot, where you can collect and destroy them.
**Grow awned varieties where you can.** PhilRice notes that awned varieties resist the bug, and panicles that stay longer inside the leaf sheath get some protection too.

**Protect natural enemies.** Small wasps such as Gryon nixoni and long horned grasshoppers kill the eggs. Spiders, crickets and lady beetles eat nymphs and adults, and the fungus Beauveria bassiana infects them.

blocks.title: Spraying too much brings pests back
blocks.text: IRRI warns that careless insecticide use kills the wasps and spiders that hold pests down, and then the pests return in bigger numbers. The [brown planthopper](/problems/brown-planthopper) is the classic example in rice.
Chemical control: Alika, Karate and lambda cyhalothrin

PhilRice advises using a pesticide only when the count calls for it and asking an agricultural extension worker first. If your counts pass the threshold, choose a product whose FPA registered label lists this pest on rice.

Two familiar examples come from Syngenta. The Karate insecticide (Karate 2.5 EC) contains lambda cyhalothrin, a pyrethroid in IRAC Group 3A. Its Philippine product page names rice bug on rice, along with leaffolder, black bugs, armyworms and green leafhopper. The Alika insecticide (Alika 247 ZC) mixes lambda cyhalothrin with thiamethoxam, a Group 4A neonicotinoid, and its page lists rice bug, stem borer and leafhoppers on rice.

Both are broad spectrum products, so they can also kill spiders and other friendly insects. Read the whole label before you mix: the rate per tank, the number of sprays, the pre harvest interval and the protective gear. Rice bugs feed until the grain hardens, close to harvest, so the pre harvest interval deserves extra care. Our guides to [Alika, Virtako and Chess](/blog/rice-insecticides-alika-virtako-chess) and to [Karate, Cymbush and Selecron](/blog/karate-cymbush-selecron-insecticides) compare these products, and the [FPA guide](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority) explains how to check a registration.

items.q: What is the rice bug called in Tagalog?
items.a: PhilRice gives atangya as the Tagalog name and dangaw as the Ilocano name. One Camarines Sur source gives tayangaw. Tagalog dictionaries use alitangya for the rice black bug, so look at the insect before you decide.
From just before flowering to the soft dough stage, while the grains hold milky sap. PhilRice puts that window at about 30 days.

items.q: Are rice bugs and rice black bugs the same?
items.a: No. The rice bug is slender and feeds on milky grains in the panicle. The rice black bug is a round, dark stink bug that sucks sap at the base of the plant and can cause deadhearts and bugburn.
No. Count first. IRRI says direct control may be needed when you find more than 10 bugs in 20 hills. PhilRice says not to let the count pass 5 nymphs and adults per square meter at the milky stage.

items.q: Which insecticide works on rice bugs?
items.a: Karate and Alika, both with lambda cyhalothrin, list rice bug on rice on their Philippine product pages. Treat them as examples, use only FPA registered products and follow the label.
